issues.item: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a 57-year-old male with a life-threatening accident, 'people who look similar to the victims' is hard to reconcile unless multiple identifiable victims were involved; this reads more like an interpersonal/assault or disaster context than a typical accident-based trigger profile.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies shame/visible mark/social exposure concerns that are not supported by the rest of the selected profile. With no memory, threat, or strategy items linking to visible injury or interpersonal scrutiny, this appraisal does not fit coherently with the accident-focused triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control
issues.explanation: The profile is not clinically coherent because the formulation specifies no active edges between nodes, implying the selected nodes should not form a tightly linked PTSD pattern. However, the trigger 'Lack of control' and the appraisal 'I can no longer trust my own body' are naturally connected in a life-threatening accident presentation, and the appraisal set itself forms a strong post-traumatic meaning cluster rather than isolated components.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, the items are not contradictory, but they cluster around severe global defeat/disconnection ('Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore', 'I feel dead inside') plus somatic mistrust after accident trauma ('I can no longer trust my own body'). This is clinically plausible on its own, but together with the trigger content it implies an integrated trauma formulation that conflicts with the fully disconnected edge structure.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because the cognitive formulation specifies no active edges at all, yet the selected Triggers and Negative Appraisals imply a linked trauma network. Concrete accident reminders (car sounds, crash imagery, temperature on skin) would ordinarily connect to threat, memory, or appraisals; presenting them alongside strong post-traumatic self-appraisals without any connecting nodes is inconsistent with the formulation structure.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within the available nodes, the Negative Appraisals are internally coherent, and the Triggers are broadly plausible for a life-threatening accident. The main problem is cross-node/formulation mismatch: specific sensory accident triggers and severe trauma-related appraisals are both present, but the formulation says these components are not linked to each other or to any other PTSD processes.

vignette:
David had built his fifty-seven years on a foundation of control and aesthetic precision. As an interior designer, his reputation rested on his ability to walk into a chaotic space and see its potential, to command lines, colours, and textures into a harmonious whole. His own body had always felt like an extension of this principle: reliable, strong, and subject to his will. This sense of mastery vanished seven months ago on a rain-slicked stretch of interstate. He remembers the squeal of tires from the car that hydroplaned across three lanes, the sickening crunch of metal, and a brief, crystalline thought that this was how it would end. He survived the collision, but the man who left the hospital after weeks of surgery on his shattered femur was someone David no longer recognized.

In the months that followed, the world outside his apartment became a landscape of threats. Driving to a client’s showroom, a task he once performed on autopilot, is now a white-knuckle ordeal. The sound of a car horn or the sudden hiss of air brakes can cause him to flinch so violently he has to pull over, heart hammering against his ribs. He finds himself scanning the road not for traffic patterns, but for signs of past violence—the scarred guardrail, the shimmer of broken glass on the shoulder, the tell-tale dent in another car’s bumper. Last month, while meeting with a new client, another designer began recounting a story about a recent fender-bender. David had to abruptly excuse himself, walking out of the potentially lucrative meeting with a flimsy excuse about a forgotten appointment, unable to bear the casual discussion of something that felt so monumental to him.

David also grapples with a profound shift in his sense of self. He is keenly aware of the slight limp that remains from his injury, a constant, physical reminder of his body’s fragility. He has come to believe that he can no longer trust his own body, that it is a fragile machine that failed him once and could catastrophically fail him again at any moment. This physical uncertainty has bled into a deeper, more unsettling feeling of alienation. He looks at his portfolio, at the bold, confident designs he created before the accident, and feels a complete disconnect, as if they were the work of a stranger. He feels he does not know himself anymore; the decisive, energetic man who built a successful business over three decades seems to have been replaced by this hesitant, frightened shell. He is certain that he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the core of his identity was shattered in the impact and can never be reassembled.

These changes have hollowed out his life. He turns down projects in distant suburbs, unable to face the long drives, and his once-thriving business is beginning to falter. Friends who try to connect find him distant and irritable, particularly if the conversation veers anywhere near current events that might involve accidents or injuries. His ex-wife called last week, concerned after hearing from a mutual acquaintance that he had missed a major industry event. He was short with her, unable to explain the dread that had kept him at home, staring at the wall. He came to therapy after losing his oldest client; he had cancelled their last three meetings, each time inventing a new excuse for why he couldn't make the crosstown drive to their home. He sat in the waiting room, his gaze fixed on the floor, finally admitting to himself that he was losing everything he had worked for. He is terrified that his belief is correct—that the best parts of him were permanently lost in the wreckage, and that there is nothing left to salvage.
